events/yoido-full-gospel-church-1958/sum: David Yonggi Cho and Choi Ja-shil began a tent church in a Seoul slum in 1958 preaching healing, prosperity and the 'fourfold gospel'. Moving to Yeouido island in 1973 and organised through cell groups, it grew to some 800,000 members by the 2000s, the largest congregation in the world.
events/mekane-yesus-founded-1959/title: Founding of the Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus
events/mekane-yesus-founded-1959/summary: Congregations founded by Scandinavian, German and American Lutheran missions, together with Ethiopian evangelical believers, united as an autonomous national church in January 1959, taking the name of the Addis Ababa congregation 'Mekane Yesus' ('Place of Jesus').
events/mekane-yesus-founded-1959/causes/: Growth of evangelical congregations especially in western and southern Ethiopia
Missions' commitment to an autonomous Ethiopian church
events/mekane-yesus-founded-1959/consequ: Rapid growth into one of the world's largest Lutheran churches
Persecution under the Derg; murder of General Secretary Gudina Tumsa (1979)
events/korean-presbyterian-split-1959/ti: Division of the Presbyterian Church of Korea (Tonghap and Hapdong)
events/korean-presbyterian-split-1959/su: At its 44th General Assembly in Daejeon (1959) the Presbyterian Church of Korea divided into the Tonghap ('united') and Hapdong ('joint') denominations. The disputes centred on membership in the World Council of Churches, theological direction and a controversy over a seminary land purchase.
events/korean-presbyterian-split-1959/ca: Earlier splits over the Shinto shrine issue (Kosin, 1952) and biblical criticism (Kijang, 1953)
events/korean-presbyterian-split-1959/co: Two large Presbyterian denominations of comparable size
Proliferation of further Korean Presbyterian bodies
events/charismatic-renewal-1960/title: Charismatic renewal begins in historic churches
events/charismatic-renewal-1960/summary: Episcopal rector Dennis Bennett's announcement on Passion Sunday 1960 that he had spoken in tongues marked the public start of the charismatic movement in mainline churches. Catholic renewal followed at Duquesne University in 1967; by the 1980s charismatics were found in nearly every tradition.
events/charismatic-renewal-1960/causes/0: Pentecostal influence through Full Gospel Business Men
events/genesis-flood-1961/title: The Genesis Flood launches modern creationism
events/genesis-flood-1961/summary: John C. Whitcomb and Henry M. Morris published The Genesis Flood, reviving the flood geology of the Seventh-day Adventist George McCready Price for a broad evangelical audience. It sparked the “creation science” movement, the Institute for Creation Research (1970), Answers in Genesis (1994) and creationist organisations from Korea to Brazil.
events/genesis-flood-1961/consequences/0: Young-earth creationism became the majority view among American evangelicals for decades
events/genesis-flood-1961/consequences/1: Legal battles over “balanced treatment” (McLean v. Arkansas 1982, Edwards v. Aguillard 1987)
events/uganda-province-1961/title: Inauguration of the Province of Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi
events/uganda-province-1961/summary: The Anglican dioceses of Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, rooted in the Church Missionary Society mission begun in 1877, became a self-governing province in 1961, with Leslie Brown as first archbishop; Erica Sabiti became the first African archbishop in 1966.
events/uganda-province-1961/causes/0: Growth of the CMS church and the East African Revival (from the 1930s)
events/uganda-province-1961/consequences: Archbishop Janani Luwum's murder under Idi Amin (1977)
events/second-vatican-council-1962/summa: Called by John XXIII for aggiornamento (updating), some 2,500 bishops from every continent produced sixteen documents on liturgy, revelation, the church and the modern world. Vernacular liturgy, collegiality, religious freedom, ecumenism and a new stance toward Judaism and other religions reshaped global Catholicism.
events/second-vatican-council-1962/longT: Vatican II was the first truly global council, with bishops from Africa, Asia and Latin America and observers from Orthodox and Protestant churches. Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963) called for 'full, conscious and active participation' and opened the way for vernacular Mass. Dei Verbum taught that Scripture and Tradition form one sacred deposit and encouraged biblical scholarship. Lumen Gentium described the church as the people of God and a sacrament of salvation, affirmed episcopal collegiality and the universal call to holiness, and said the church of Christ 'subsists in' the Catholic Church while elements of truth exist beyond it. Unitatis Redintegratio called other Christians 'separated brethren'; Nostra Aetate repudiated blaming Jews collectively for Christ's death; Dignitatis Humanae affirmed religious freedom; Gaudium et Spes engaged the modern world. Interpretation remains contested: progressives saw an unfinished revolution, traditionalists (notably Archbishop Lefebvre) a rupture, and Popes Benedict XVI and Francis spoke of a 'hermeneutic of reform' in continuity. Many Protestants welcomed the Bible-centred liturgy and ecumenical openness while noting that core doctrinal differences remained.
events/sacrosanctum-concilium-1963/summa: Vatican II’s first promulgated document (4 December 1963) calls for the "full, conscious, and active participation" of the faithful, wider use of vernacular languages, restoration of the rites to noble simplicity, a richer reading of Scripture and adaptation to cultures.
events/sacrosanctum-concilium-1963/cause: Pius XII’s Mediator Dei (1947) and Holy Week reforms (1955)
events/nostra-aetate-1965/summary: Vatican II’s declaration on non-Christian religions (28 October 1965) states that the Jews as a people cannot be charged with Christ’s death, that they remain dear to God for the sake of the patriarchs, and that the Church deplores antisemitism; it also speaks respectfully of Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism.
events/nostra-aetate-1965/causes/1: John XXIII’s meeting with Jules Isaac (1960)
events/nostra-aetate-1965/consequences/1: Revision of catechetical teaching about Jews
events/dignitatis-humanae-1965/summary: Vatican II’s declaration on religious freedom (7 December 1965) affirms that every person has a right, grounded in human dignity, to be free from coercion in religious matters, privately and publicly, within just limits; it was largely drafted with John Courtney Murray and contested by a conservative minority.
events/dignitatis-humanae-1965/causes/1: American and Eastern European bishops’ experience
events/dignitatis-humanae-1965/consequen: Catholic support for religious liberty and democracy (the "third wave" of democratisation)
events/chinese-cultural-revolution-1966/: Mao's Cultural Revolution closed all churches, including Three-Self ones; Bibles were burned and clergy sent to labour camps. Christianity survived in secret home gatherings and, after 1979, emerged much larger, especially in rural house-church networks.
events/humanae-vitae-1968/summary: Paul VI’s encyclical (25 July 1968), overruling the majority of his own advisory commission, teaches that each marital act must remain open to the transmission of life and condemns artificial contraception, while permitting the use of infertile periods for serious reasons. It provoked unprecedented public dissent from theologians and some bishops’ conferences.
events/humanae-vitae-1968/consequences/1: John Paul II’s Theology of the Body (1979–84)
events/medellin-conference-1968/title: Medellín Conference of Latin American bishops
events/medellin-conference-1968/summary: The second general conference of CELAM applied Vatican II to a continent of poverty and dictatorship, denouncing 'institutionalised violence' and endorsing base ecclesial communities and a preferential concern for the poor. It gave momentum to liberation theology, formulated by Gustavo Gutiérrez in 1971.
events/united-methodist-union-1968/title: Union forms the United Methodist Church
events/united-methodist-union-1968/summa: On 23 April 1968 in Dallas the Methodist Church and the Evangelical United Brethren Church united as the United Methodist Church. The same General Conference abolished the segregated Central Jurisdiction (created in 1939) that had grouped Black Methodist conferences separately.
events/united-methodist-union-1968/cause: Shared Wesleyan and German Pietist heritage of the two churches
Pressure of the civil rights movement against the Central Jurisdiction
events/united-methodist-union-1968/conse: Largest mainline Protestant church in the U.S. for decades
1972 language declaring homosexual practice incompatible with Christian teaching began a fifty-year dispute
events/ancient-church-of-the-east-1968/t: Consecration of Mar Thoma Darmo and the Ancient Church of the East
events/ancient-church-of-the-east-1968/s: Opposition to Patriarch Mar Eshai Shimun XXIII's adoption of the Gregorian calendar (1964) and to hereditary patriarchal succession led a party in Iraq to consecrate Mar Thoma Darmo, metropolitan in India, as a rival patriarch in Baghdad in 1968.
events/ancient-church-of-the-east-1968/c: Long-standing objections to uncle-to-nephew patriarchal succession
Patriarch's residence in exile in the United States
Ancient Church of the East with a Baghdad-based patriarchate
Ongoing reconciliation talks with the Assyrian Church of the East
events/missal-of-paul-vi-1969/summary: Paul VI promulgates the revised Order of Mass (apostolic constitution Missale Romanum, 3 April 1969), in use from Advent 1969: a three-year lectionary, new eucharistic prayers, the prayers of the faithful and celebration in vernacular languages.
events/church-of-north-india-1970/title: Inauguration of the Church of North India at Nagpur
events/church-of-north-india-1970/summar: On 29 November 1970 six churches — the United Church of Northern India (Presbyterian and Congregational), the Anglican Church of India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon (northern dioceses), the Council of Baptist Churches in Northern India, the Methodist Church (British and Australian conferences), the Church of the Brethren in India and the Disciples of Christ — united as the Church of North India.
events/church-of-north-india-1970/causes: Example of the Church of South India (1947)
Missionary and Indian desire to end imported Western divisions
events/church-of-north-india-1970/conseq: First union to include Baptists and to reconcile believers' and infant baptism within one church
Full communion with the Anglican Communion and member of the World Methodist Council and WCRC
The Church of Pakistan formed the same year
events/oca-autocephaly-1970/title: Moscow grants autocephaly to the Orthodox Church in America
events/oca-autocephaly-1970/summary: In April 1970 the Moscow Patriarchate granted autocephaly to the former Russian Orthodox 'Metropolia' in North America, which took the name Orthodox Church in America. The Ecumenical Patriarchate and several other churches did not recognise the act, holding that only Constantinople may grant autocephaly in the diaspora.
events/oca-autocephaly-1970/causes/0: Decades of separation between the American Metropolia and Moscow after 1917
events/oca-autocephaly-1970/causes/1: Desire for a single, local, English-speaking American Orthodox church
events/oca-autocephaly-1970/consequences: Recognition by Moscow and some churches (e.g. Bulgaria, Georgia, Poland, Czech Lands and Slovakia) but not by Constantinople
Ongoing debate over 'diaspora' jurisdiction and canonical territory
